projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with George E. McMillen was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran, George E. McMillen. Mr. McMillen served in the U.S. Army with the 143rd AAA Gun Battalion, Battery C. He served in the European theatre and his highest rank was T5. I'm Tom Swope and this interview was recorded in the lobby of a hotel near Columbus, Ohio, at the reunion of the 143rd AAA Battalion on July 20th, 2003. George was 91 at the time of this recording. So where were you living in 1941? Burbank?

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: No. In '41 -- I was married in 1938. We just celebrated our 65th wedding anniversary yesterday here, coming here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: Oh, definitely, definitely.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tell me what you remember about that.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: I lived on 928 West 83rd Street in a house -- in an apartment we rented. I had a car, a garage off of the alley, and I just had bought a new Plymouth. I was out there in the garage that Sunday morning cleaning it or doing something with the radio -- which was very rare on it -- on, and the news came over of the attack on Pearl Harbor. And all our lives changed from that moment on.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did you personally think when you heard that news?

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: Oh, I was horrified, I was horrified, like everybody else, of course. No television in those days, but everybody ran to their radios and listened to all the news and heard the President Roosevelt make his big speech I think the next day, if I remember right, and everything changed from then on.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure. And you were married at the time --

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: I was married.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- and so you probably weren't going to be drafted.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: I didn't expect to be. That was the biggest surprise I had. I was 31 years old. I had been married for four years, and I had a son. I still got drafted.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You still got. So when were you --

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: They were at the bottom of the barrel. You know that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when was that you were drafted? That was --

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: April -- April -- sometime around the middle of April of 1943.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So age 31, wife and child, you were drafted.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: April, '43.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: Right. I heard many people say, Oh, you're lucky. You didn't get in the service because you were a married man. Well, that's not true.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: There was a cutoff date in there sometime just shortly before that. I think I just missed it by -- I can't remember what that date was but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: I debated a long time before then -- I worked in a bank. That's where I started out in 1935 -- whether I should quit my job and go to work in the defense industry and avoid the draft. But I had an older brother and a younger brother that were both in the service so I kind of felt obligated. So I survived it and I'm glad I did.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: A lot of nice guys that I know now.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You trained at Camp Haan then.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any stories you remember from your training?

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: Oh, not too much. I went in the 122nd the first time, and it was -- consisted of men from the southern California area. Like the 143rd is mostly people -- or men from this area more or less. So I knew some of them from school and from work and what not. And then you go through all this training and checking you for this and that. And it turned out I had good scarious scopic vision. You know what that is. It means you have the perception of depth.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: And that was the only qualification to become a height finder observer. So I was sent from that -- from the 122nd back to North Carolina to Camp Davis to go through height finder school, which I think consisted of two or three months, something like that. And then when I finished school, why I was sent back to California; and the 143rd was in the same week of basic training that I'd left in the other one. So that's how I was assigned to 143rd. And I joined them a few days after Thanksgiving in 1943. And then from then on, why the story is what you've heard a lot about.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right. Well, go ahead and tell me from there. Tell me about your impressions of the trip overseas.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: Well, yeah. We went over on the Highland Brigade. We left from New York. Because Battery C in a competition before we left of some kind, we came up pretty good. So we were in the -- C was assigned to assist the British crew in manning the aircraft guns and what not on the ship. And my assignment was on -- like Pete just told you, he was on the front, I was on the stern on the port side and something built out over the edge. We had guns similar to R-50s. They had another name for them. And we'd shift, you know. You were on two or four and off eight or something like that. So one night when I was on my shift out there, cold North Atlantic weather, and there's a vibration from the propellers and a sound because we were over the edge a few feet, why I overheard -- something told me it didn't sound right, you know, and it was foggy, couldn't see anything, and I kept staring out. And all of a sudden right within two or three feet of me was the bow of another ship. We were in a convoy, of course, and so I didn't know what to do. So there was regular British sailors on duty back there, too. I hollered at one of them to come over, and he saw it. And so then he alerted the bridge in some way, and pretty soon we separated. But I could almost touch the bow of that other ship. That's how close they were. Visibility was practically zero. So that was one thing that happened. And then the rest of the event was rather uneventful, slow, and we never saw any subs or anything like that, but we had lots of escort ships and what not sailing around. And when we got to England in, oh, what's the town inland there, the port?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Southampton?

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: No. That's where we left from.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, that's where you left from.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: Up by -- in the midlands.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Not Liverpool.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: Yeah, Liverpool. We landed outside the Liverpool, but we couldn't get in for a couple of days to dock because there's a break water or something, the tide had to be right, and there was other ships there. So we stayed on board, I think, a couple of days until we got in to dock. They took us off and we went to this camp not too far from there where we assembled all of our equipment. But we didn't take anything with us. And I had my wife -- her mother was born in England and she had lots of relatives over there. And I was hoping to get away to visit, but I never did at that time. And then when we finally left for Southampton after, I don't know, a few weeks there and spent about two or three days at a big park outside of Southampton; and during then our guys, I don't know where they found it, but they found a warehouse or something full of potatoes. And we came back and took five-gallon cans and put lard in them or oil and we made French fries. And we ate homemade French fries for a couple of days before we went. And we finally -- they boarded the LSTs, and we set sail the middle of the night across the channel. Our truck -- we had a special truck and I was on a height finder which is an optical instrument for calculating slant range and elevation of aircraft. And it was a long tube, about 13 or 14 feet long, so we had to have a special vehicle to haul that. So we had the only long bedded truck in the whole outfit. And, of course, the crew all traveled in there, too. So we crossed the channel that night in the back of that truck. Every place we went we were in the back of that truck.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: And by about daylight or so we landed on the beach, and they had bulldozers and what not there to build up a berm when they put the ramp down so that we could drive off. So I went on the shore without -- I never got my feet wet. I never got out of the truck. Once we got off the ship, they wouldn't even let us stop. They took us inland to the staging area two or three miles away. So it was rather quick and uneventful, I must say, which made it good; but the shooting by the time we got there in late August was gone. And then we spent two or three days -- a couple of days in a farmer's pasture waiting for orders and where to go. And then when they did come through, they sent us to Paris; and you've heard the story how we got into this victory garden in St-Denis, this victory garden of people who owned their -- or at least grew their crops there all had tool sheds or something like that. So we took those over. They were pretty small. But we got some lumber from a German supply depot that we found someplace. And in large -- we had a nice comfortable dry place. I think there was six of us, I believe, that lived in there for as long as we were there, which was a couple of months before we moved on to Versailles.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You didn't have much air opposition at that point from the German Air Force.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: No. We manned all the equipment on the thing, but we didn't have any air operation.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you moved to Versailles.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: We were there for Thanksgiving dinner. We were there a short time. And then while we were eating Thanksgiving dinner orders came through that we were to go to Belgium, Liege, I believe it was, but I'm not positive if it was that area. We were in so many different sites there. We moved up there, and then from there we went to numerous places and then into Germany through Ogden.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What do you remember about the opening days of the Battle of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: Well, I was -- as I say, I was in the -- the -- we call it the range section. We're the guys that didn't man guns. We aimed them primarily. That was it. And so there was really not much for us to do when we were shooting the tanks, you know, nothing to do.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Because your job was for anti-aircraft.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: Yeah. Right. So we all ended up in security.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Guarding the guns, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: No. Well, we manned -- we helped man the machine guns for our own security, yeah, but mostly we'd be out on the patrol where guns were set up because there were all kinds of things going on. So that's what I did during the time that the Battle of the Bulge was on when we were in Spa. See, that's Belgium. That's Belgium, I think, the town of Spa. We were there at Christmastime in 1944 I guess it was.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: And we had -- our cooks were there, and they were supposed to prepare meals and take them out to all the guys manning the guns, you know, in the front. The night that they received a bunch of frozen chickens for our -- I mean turkeys for our Christmas meal, and the cooks -- I don't know what they got ahold of but something. They all got drunk the night before. And when it come time to cook the chickens, they cooked them but they didn't clean them. So you can imagine eating a turkey dinner that's everything in there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And everything on the inside, yeah, I know.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: It spoiled the whole thing. So we ended up having neither K rations or C rations for our chicken for our Christmas dinner. I think there was a few -- a few guys got busted over that. And then after Christmas, why the Battle of the Bulge ended; and pretty soon -- I've forgotten the date of the armistice when we actually -- but we were there from then until -- well, after that I got called into the office one day and told that I was going to be sent to Paris to attend a de-arming school, I think it was how to de-arm bug things that they've -- what's the word I want? Booby traps --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. Right.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: -- that kind of stuff.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: So I went to this school which was at a university in Paris. I think it was like a couple of weeks. And that wasn't too bad. That was pretty good because I was living in a dorm and they had a beautiful cafeteria and things that we weren't used to, you know. At night you were free to go out in Paris and do whatever you wanted. So I enjoyed that. Then one night we went back to our own outfit and thank God I never one time got called on to go out and do what he did, --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: -- looking for bugs or anything like that. I don't know why I was selected because I was not a gunner or anything, but I was. But I remember that well.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else come to mind?

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: Well, from then on, after we went back to and they broke up the -- the war was over and the armistice was signed and all that; and everybody was assigned a number, you know, for -- to return. And because I had entered the service several months before the 143rd, why I had a little bit higher number. And so most of our guys, almost all them, were shipped out to other groups to return with. And the 143rd turned out to be the exact number that I had. So I stayed there with them. And the company clerk had left and I was his assistant during most of that time, and I ended up being the guy that did all the office work and bringing all the things back on the ship. So I brought that clear back, the records and stuff that we had, clear back to New York. I got there just a couple of days before Christmas in 1945, and I spent Christmas in the camp, whatever it was, hoping -- waiting for transportation back to California where they flew us back on a shuttle bus on a DC-3. It only hold about 22, 23 people -- passengers, you know. And we left New York on the -- either the 26th or the 27th, right after Christmas, at night from an air field in New Jersey, and we flew from there to Dayton, Ohio, in the worst storm I've ever been in. We were only flying about 200 feet high so they could see the road and the car lights and everything in this old, old DC-3 or whatever they called it.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: Yeah. C-47. Which would have been a cargo plane. There was no lining in it. It was just metal inside and all the wires and tubes and everything. And it would freeze up so it was so cold; and when you got in warmer weather, it would melt. So we had to wear rain coats all during that trip to keep from getting soaked. We finally got to Dayton about 2, 3:00 in the morning and landed where they had cleared the runway, went into the USO, and got coffee and all of that, used the rest room. Then we took off a couple hours later for, I think it was Memphis or someplace down that way, and good beautiful weather with the moon shining, did the same stop again there, and in daylight we headed west, went to Dallas, same thing, from Dallas to Phoenix, got in there late in the afternoon because these things moved so slow that it took us a long time. And from there we flew into Long Beach, California, got in there about dark on the 27th of December, 1945. And then the truck took us over to San Pedro to Fort MacArthur where the reception center had been. And two days -- first got there in the evening on the 27th, and our discharge procedure didn't start for two days. So they assigned you a place to sleep if you wanted to stay; but of course my home was only an hour away, so I took off. One of the permanent men, one of the sergeants that worked down there, had a big old Buick; and for a few bucks he'd drive you to LA every night. So I got in with others and headed north. I got off at 54th and Figuero Street because my home was on 832 West 54th, just two blocks from where my parents lived. I walked in and opened the door and walked in on them. Nobody knew I was back. And then after greeting them, why my brother was there, drove me back up to Hollywood where my wife and son was. Then I had two days off. Then I had a car there. So then I went back to San Pedro to start my discharge procedure, one whole day. And the next day, which was on the 31st of December, 1945, about noon I got my final, went and had lunch; and that ended my military career.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You had a nice reunion with your wife when you got back?

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: That night my friends had planned a big party. It was New Year's Eve. So we had a combination New Year's Eve party and welcome home party. I remember that well. Happiest day of my life I think almost.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experiences during the war, does any vivid memory come to mind, any one thing or more than one thing?

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: Oh, not really. I didn't have any really bad experiences or anything or didn't get hurt or sick or anything. I was really fortunate.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have close buddies over there, overseas?

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: Well, just the group that --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The guys that are here?

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: All these guys, yeah. We all became friends.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any buddies over there?

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: Nah. We lost a couple of guys, but they were not real close friends of mine. I lost a lot of them since.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: And I kept in touch with about five or six of them, usually Christmastime, you know, with Christmas cards; and some of them are still here today. But I've lost two or three or four of those now, so it's down to just a small group. Yep.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you think that covers it?

sp.speaker: George E. McMillen
sp.p: That covers it.
